title: SEBI's GARUDA Framework Slashes Fund Launch Times, Opening a Faster Path for India's Startup Investors
excerpt: India's markets regulator approved a new fast-track mechanism that cuts Alternative Investment Fund scheme launches from 30 days to 10, signaling a shift toward speed and self-certification in the world's third-largest startup ecosystem.
body:
• SEBI's new GARUDA framework cuts Alternative Investment Fund scheme launch timelines from 30 days to as little as 10 working days, with accredited investor-only schemes eligible for near-immediate launch.
  • The reform shifts India's approach from lengthy pre-launch regulatory reviews to a disclosure-led model with greater fund manager accountability and post-facto supervision.
  • India's AIF industry has grown to 1,849 registered funds with cumulative commitments of ₹15.74 lakh crore, up from 732 funds five years ago.
  • For NRI investors allocating capital to Indian startups through VC and PE funds, the reform removes one of the longest-standing friction points in the investment process.

What GARUDA Changes

The Securities and Exchange Board of India approved the GARUDA framework — Green-Channel: AIF Rollout Upon Document Acknowledgement — on June 19, 2026, through amendments to the SEBI (Alternative Investment Funds) Regulations, 2012. The mechanism creates a fast-track pathway for launching new fund schemes, replacing the previous system that could leave capital waiting for weeks or months before deployment.

Under the old rules, fund managers had to file a private placement memorandum through a merchant banker and wait at least 30 days before launching a scheme. GARUDA compresses that to 10 working days for regular schemes. Accredited investor-only schemes and angel funds get an even faster lane — they can launch immediately after filing, without a merchant banker due diligence certificate.

The framework does not distinguish between AIF categories. Whether a venture capital fund under Category I, a private equity fund under Category II, or a hedge fund under Category III, the speed of approval now depends on the sophistication of the investors, not the type of fund.

Why Timing Matters for Startups

In venture capital, weeks can make the difference between winning and losing a deal. A fund that cannot deploy capital quickly risks watching competitors close rounds on promising companies. The previous approval timeline — particularly when SEBI sought clarifications that could stretch the process well beyond 30 days — created a structural disadvantage for Indian-domiciled funds competing against global investors who faced no such delays.

""Once you're a SEBI-registered manager, launching a new fund or scheme can be a much more routine process," he said."

"Foreign investors have often found it difficult to understand the time involved in launching AIF schemes in India," said Archana Jahagirdar, founder and managing partner at Rukam Capital. "A more streamlined and predictable approval process can significantly enhance India's attractiveness as an investment destination."

Pranav Pai, managing partner at 3one4 Capital, noted that GARUDA aligns India with how mature markets operate. "Once you're a SEBI-registered manager, launching a new fund or scheme can be a much more routine process," he said. "In most mature markets, once the manager is licensed and the investors are accredited, the emphasis is on disclosures and accountability rather than repeated approvals."

The Trade-Off: Speed for Accountability

The faster approvals come with a catch. SEBI is shifting from detailed pre-launch scrutiny to post-facto supervision. Fund managers must now provide certifications and undertakings that their scheme documents are accurate and compliant. Any misstatements or lapses will attract regulatory action after the fact, rather than being caught during a lengthy review process.

"GARUDA helps in scheme launches, but fund managers still need to comply with a large number of regulatory requirements. If some of the non-essential compliances can be eased, it would be particularly beneficial for smaller funds."

— Anil Joshi, Managing Partner, Unicorn India Ventures

This mirrors a broader global trend in financial regulation: trusting regulated entities to self-certify upfront, then auditing them rigorously afterward. The approach recognizes that accredited investors — institutions and high-net-worth individuals — can evaluate risks on their own without extensive regulatory hand-holding.

The Bigger Picture for NRI Investors

India's alternative investment industry has grown rapidly. The number of registered AIFs has risen to 1,849 as of March 2026, up from 732 five years ago. Cumulative commitments stand at ₹15.74 lakh crore (approximately $188 billion), with net investments reaching ₹6.45 lakh crore as of December 2025.

For NRIs investing in India's startup ecosystem — either directly through angel fund schemes or through VC and PE vehicles — GARUDA removes a practical bottleneck. Faster fund launches mean quicker capital deployment into the pipeline of Indian startups that increasingly compete on a global stage. India's startup ecosystem, the world's third-largest, produced 96 unicorn founders in the United States alone, according to a recent National Foundation for American Policy report.

The reform also arrives as India pursues broader capital market modernization. SEBI has simultaneously introduced a formal recusal framework for its senior officials and proposed tighter monitoring of how companies use funds raised through public offerings — moves that signal a regulator trying to balance speed with integrity.

What Comes Next

GARUDA may not solve every challenge in India's alternative investment landscape. Fund managers still face substantial ongoing compliance costs, and smaller funds disproportionately feel that burden. But by removing the launch-day bottleneck, SEBI has addressed one of the industry's oldest complaints.

The real test will be whether faster approvals translate into measurably faster capital deployment — and whether the post-facto enforcement regime is rigorous enough to maintain investor confidence without the safety net of pre-launch reviews.
